## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. All finite groups with the same number of elements of each order have the same exponent.

**Definitions.** For a finite group $G$, the *exponent* of $G$ is
$$\exp(G) = \operatorname{lcm}\{\,\operatorname{ord}(g) : g \in G\,\},$$
the least common multiple of the orders of all elements of $G$.

**Setup.** Suppose $G$ and $H$ are finite groups with the same number of elements of each order. That is, for every positive integer $n$,
$$\bigl|\{g \in G : \operatorname{ord}(g) = n\}\bigr| = \bigl|\{h \in H : \operatorname{ord}(h) = n\}\bigr|.$$

**Key observation.** Define the *order spectrum* of a group $G$ as
$$S(G) = \{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \text{there exists } g \in G \text{ with } \operatorname{ord}(g) = n\}.$$
Since $G$ and $H$ have the same count of elements of each order, an order $n$ occurs in $G$ if and only if it occurs in $H$ (both counts are positive simultaneously, or both are zero). Therefore
$$S(G) = S(H).$$

**Conclusion.** The exponent depends only on the order spectrum:
$$\exp(G) = \operatorname{lcm}\bigl(S(G)\bigr) = \operatorname{lcm}\bigl(S(H)\bigr) = \exp(H).$$

Thus $G$ and $H$ have the same exponent. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
